text: Retrieval-augmented generation looks like an AI feature from the outside, but underneath it's a document-retrieval system with a language model summarizing the results. That reframes the security problem entirely: the hard questions aren't new AI questions, they're the same access-control and untrusted-input questions you'd ask about any system that lets a user query a document store — they're just easy to miss because asking a question doesn't look like a data-access request.

Security controls belong at every stage. At ingestion, validate and scope every document before it's indexed. At indexing, tag each chunk with access-control metadata — a tenant ID or group field — and treat that tagging with the same rigor as a column that drives row-level security, because that's exactly the role it plays. At retrieval, enforce that tag as a required filter inside the similarity search itself. At generation, treat every chunk that comes back as untrusted data, never as an instruction.

Here's the defect that shows up most often in real RAG systems: running the similarity search against the whole index, then filtering unauthorized results out afterward in application code. That fails structurally — if the top matches are dominated by documents the user can't see, filtering afterward can leave nothing useful, or a filtering bug can leak a result before anyone notices. The fix is pushing the authorization check into the query itself, built from the authenticated session, never from a client- or prompt-supplied value.

Once the right chunks come back, you've got a second problem with nothing to do with permissions: that content is untrusted, because it came from a document store, not a source you can vouch for sentence by sentence. A crafted chunk can contain phrasing designed to look like an instruction — the exact indirect-prompt-injection pattern from Chapter 2, just introduced through retrieval instead of a tool call. Wrap retrieved content in explicit delimiters, scan for instruction-like phrasing, and keep real instructions structurally separate from augmented content.

In practice that means telling the system prompt explicitly that anything inside a retrieved-content block is reference material to summarize or cite, never a command to obey — regardless of what the text inside it appears to say. None of this is a guarantee on its own. It's the retrieval-stage half of the same defense-in-depth posture you already built for indirect prompt injection, and skipping it here reopens a hole you closed somewhere else in the pipeline.

A RAG pipeline is secure end to end only when access control lives inside the retrieval query and every retrieved chunk is still treated as untrusted data once it arrives. Next lesson turns to the API layer that fronts the model itself — authentication, rate limiting tuned to token cost, input size limits, and output filtering before a response ever reaches a client.
